title: Further Derivatives and Integrals

findings.finding: The review rehearses integer-power polynomials but omits the shifted fractional-power differentiation used in the inverse investigations and worked examples.
findings.breakdown: Following the explicit inverse method requires applying the power rule to a fractional exponent and differentiating a translated input; the polynomial review does not rehearse these steps.
findings.checked: p5-inverse-derivative-response, p6-investigation and p7-worked-a require fractional-power differentiation. No earlier topic precedes this opening topic.
findings.assumptions: Fractional-power differentiation and the chain rule are prior course knowledge. Calculator use does not affect this recall requirement.

repair.proposal: Append three parts to p3-review-q1: Differentiate (i) x^(1/3), (ii) (x+4)^(1/3), (iii) √(x-2). Answers: (i) (1/3)x^(-2/3), x≠0; (ii) (1/3)(x+4)^(-2/3), x≠-4; (iii) 1/[2√(x-2)], x>2. Keep the complete review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The opening review rehearses fractional powers and translated inputs before the inverse investigations.

findings.finding: Extend the inverse-gradient question to distinguish corresponding inputs from the same numerical input.
findings.breakdown: The comparison exposes why the reciprocal rule evaluates f' at f⁻¹(x).
findings.checked: For f(x)=x³+5x, f(6)=246, f'(6)=113 and f'(1)=8. Both inverse gradients follow from the taught rule; f is strictly increasing.
findings.assumptions: Only methods taught in this topic are required.

repair.proposal: Append: (b) Find f(6). Answer: 246. (c) Find (f⁻¹)'(246). Answer: 1/113. (d) Explain why (f⁻¹)'(6)=1/8 rather than 1/113. Answer: f⁻¹(6)=1, so the rule uses f'(1)=8; f'(6)=113 gives the inverse gradient at input 246.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up compares inverse gradients at corresponding inputs.

findings.finding: The topic has no opening rehearsal of ordinary trigonometric derivatives, the tangent identity or the product rule used in its introductory teaching.
findings.breakdown: Students must recall trigonometric differentiation and sec²y=1+tan²y to complete the tangent proof, then combine the new inverse-trigonometric derivative with the product rule in p13.
findings.checked: The preceding topic rehearses polynomial and inverse-function differentiation. p12 itself supplies the sine/cosine identity, principal ranges and sign reasoning, so these are excluded. The preceding topic also uses the chain rule, so a separate chain-rule review is excluded.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary trigonometric differentiation, trigonometric identities and the product rule are prior course knowledge. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Insert three short items before p12-investigation-block: (a) Differentiate sin y, cos y and tan y with respect to y. Answers: cos y, -sin y, sec²y. (b) Complete sec²y=1+____. Answer: tan²y. (c) Differentiate x sin x. Answer: sin x+x cos x. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The review rehearses the missing trigonometric prerequisites and product differentiation.

findings.finding: Extend the viewing-angle problem by lowering the picture, then expressing the optimum using its two heights.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects the numerical optimum with the product of the bottom and top heights.
findings.checked: For θ=tan⁻¹(t/x)-tan⁻¹(b/x), θ'=(t-b)(bt-x²)/[(x²+b²)(x²+t²)]. For 0<b<t and x>0, the maximum occurs at x=√(bt). The lowered picture has b=2 and t=3.
findings.assumptions: This is a Stage 6 generalisation using the topic's existing optimisation method.

repair.proposal: Append: (d) The same 1 m picture is lowered so its bottom edge is 2 m above E. Find the viewing distance that maximises its subtended angle. Answer: √6 m. (e) For bottom and top heights b and t metres above E, where 0<b<t, find the best viewing distance in terms of b and t. Answer: √(bt) m.

findings.doneWhen: The numerical follow-up precedes the short generalisation.

findings.finding: The topic omits opening rehearsal of constant-multiple integration and upper-minus-lower evaluation, both used directly in its introductory examples.
findings.breakdown: Students must recall these integration operations while learning the new inverse-trigonometric primitives.
findings.checked: p21-example-left-content extracts a constant; p21-example-right-content evaluates a primitive at two bounds. Neither operation is rehearsed in a local review or the immediately preceding differentiation topic.
findings.assumptions: These operations are prior knowledge from the listed integration booklets. Calculators are permitted by p21-theory-block.

repair.proposal: Before p21-theory-block add: (a) Find ∫3x² dx. Answer: x³+C. (b) Evaluate ∫₁²2x dx, showing substitution of both bounds. Answer: [x²]₁²=4-1=3. (c) Given ∫g(x) dx=F(x)+C, find ∫5g(x) dx. Answer: 5F(x)+C. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Both integration operations are rehearsed before the introductory examples.

findings.finding: The instruction to use substitution precedes teaching how to change the differential and integration bounds.
findings.breakdown: Numerator matching does not supply the required procedure for rewriting an integral entirely in a new variable.
findings.checked: All preceding integration teaching retains x. Explicit differential conversion and transformed bounds are introduced only in the following topic, at p31–p33. For part (a), x=u² and dx=2u du give ∫2/(1+u²) du. For part (b), u=eˣ gives ∫₁ᵉ1/(1+u²) du.
findings.assumptions: Formal integration by substitution is new in this booklet; the listed course outcomes support this interpretation.

repair.proposal: Scaffold p30-q18-a: (i) For u=√x, express x and dx in terms of u and du. Answers: x=u²; dx=2u du. (ii) Rewrite the integral entirely in u. Answer: ∫2/(1+u²) du. (iii) Integrate and back-substitute. Answer: 2tan⁻¹√x+C. Scaffold p30-q18-b: (i) For u=eˣ, express dx and e⁻ˣ in u. Answers: dx=du/u; e⁻ˣ=1/u. (ii) Convert the bounds. Answers: 1 and e. (iii) Rewrite and evaluate. Answer: ∫₁ᵉ1/(1+u²) du=tan⁻¹e-π/4.

findings.doneWhen: Students practise differential and bound conversion before being expected to execute substitution independently.

findings.finding: The supplied order places the secant-substitution application before the exercise's scaffolded trigonometric substitutions.
findings.breakdown: After algebraic shifts, p48-q10 combines a trigonometric radical, identity-based integration, angular back-substitution and an initial condition. The later questions provide intermediate trigonometric-substitution practice.
findings.checked: In the supplied order, p48-q10 follows p46-q7. p47-q8 then practises sine, tangent and cosine substitutions; p48-q9-c combines tangent substitution with a radical. Secant differentiation is already rehearsed in p40-q10. These existing questions provide the smaller repair.
findings.assumptions: The supplied sequence is the teaching order. Ordinary trigonometric identities and initial conditions are prior knowledge.

repair.proposal: Move p48-q10 after the complete p47-q8 and p48-q9 questions, so the existing trigonometric-substitution practice precedes the secant application.

findings.doneWhen: The scaffolded trigonometric substitutions and radical application precede p48-q10.

findings.finding: Extend the three-method comparison by finding an upper bound for a prescribed accumulated area.
findings.breakdown: Students use the primitive to determine a limit rather than evaluate given limits.
findings.checked: For b>0, the integral equals √(1+b²)-1. Setting it equal to 1 gives the unique positive solution b=√3.
findings.assumptions: Only substitution, definite integration and elementary algebra already available in the topic are required.

repair.proposal: Append (d): Find b>0 such that ∫₀ᵇ x/√(1+x²) dx=1. Answer: √(1+b²)-1=1, so b=√3.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up asks students to determine an integration bound.

findings.finding: Use the fourth-power identities to compare two definite integrals.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects power reduction with the disappearance of the opposite-sign cosine terms over the interval.
findings.checked: Integrating either identity over [0,π/2] gives 3π/16 because the cos 2x and cos 4x terms integrate to zero. The identities differ only in the sign of the cos 2x term.
findings.assumptions: All required identities and integration methods are available by the end of this topic.

repair.proposal: Append: (c) Evaluate ∫₀^{π/2}sin⁴x dx. Answer: 3π/16. (d) Evaluate ∫₀^{π/2}cos⁴x dx. Answer: 3π/16. (e) Using your identities, explain why the integrals are equal. Answer: their only differing term is ±½cos 2x, whose integral over this interval is zero.

findings.doneWhen: The identity question includes the two evaluations and their comparison.
